newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin wins praise, scorn at home over NATO deal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin wins praise, scorn at home over NATO deal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin either scored a late winning goal in Tuesday's diplomatic football match in Paris or was cheated with shoddy goods at the NATO bazaar -- it depended which Russian paper you read on Wednesday.

"At the Elysee Palace, they treated Russia like Yeliseyev's store, palming off rubbish in fancy packaging," ran the front page headline in communist daily Pravda-5, in a reference to aristocratic tsarist-era shops in Moscow and St Petersburg.
"Never has the security of our country suffered such serious tests," it went on, accusing Yeltsin of signing an "act of unconditional surrender" at France's Elysee presidential palace.

Opposition legislators in the "Anti-NATO" group said the "NATO-Russia Founding Act" was a defeat for Kremlin diplomacy and called for new "political, economic and military measures" to repel the threat of western influence over Russian society.
Fortunately for Yeltsin, the treaty with Moscow's old Cold War adversary does not need to be ratified by the communist-dominated parliament.

Kommersant Daily was more positive on the pact. The business newspaper reckoned the Kremlin leader stole the show -- and won the diplomatic points game -- with a surprise offer to scale back Russia's nuclear threat to NATO's 16 present members.
"NATO can't believe its ears," headlined Kommersant, saying the move, which left NATO leaders confused as to its meaning, gave Yeltsin a moral victory on the day -- "3-2 to Russia".

Like Pravda, Kommersant accepted Yeltsin had allowed the West two of its goals -- that former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe be allowed to join NATO and that NATO become a key element in European security following its Cold War victory.

But unlike the communist paper, which complained NATO assurances not to extend deployment of its nuclear and other forces were not proper guarantees, Kommersant reckoned those promises were worth a point to the Kremlin.
Getting a say in NATO affairs and a role in world bodies like the Group of Seven (G7) industrial powers -- now to be effectively the G8 -- was another goal for Moscow.

Yeltsin's apparently off-the-cuff intervention during Tuesday's signing ceremony, saying nuclear missiles aimed at NATO countries would "have their warheads removed", caught both his fellow leaders and his own delegation off guard.
"No one could believe the Russian president could do such a thing," commented liberal daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.

Hasty explanations by officials later made it clear that what he meant to say was that Russia would stop the permanent targetting of missiles against the West -- which would not prevent Russia launching a rapid atomic strike if it wanted.
"It would appear that, to a large degree, this sensational announcement by Yeltsin should be treated as a purely political gesture," Nezavisimaya said.

But Kommersant reckoned the gesture was a last-minute winner for Russia: "After Boris Yeltsin's announcement...whether or not it is really carried out, any NATO challenges will be seen quite simply as breaches of international rules of decency."
Pavel Felgengauer, defence analyst with the Sevodnya liberal newspaper, considered the confusion over what Yeltsin, the head of Russia's armed forces, actually meant.
He concluded it would have no impact on defence.
"Nonetheless, Yeltsin's 'slip of the tongue' in Paris points to a serious danger -- the commander-in-chief understands absolutely nothing about military affairs," Felgengauer wrote.
